about: THE PEOPLE OF THE ENCOUNTERS (Design/npc_text_encounters.md 2.5): what kind of person fills each role (a fixed role is the same person at a port every call, until they die and an heir takes it), each people's tongue and faith, each realm's and port's peoples, and the words for how a person feels toward the merchant. Extended 4 Oct 2026 by the spine (Design/content/spine.json), which alone may add to it: every role the content uses, the peoples a writer may name, and a row for each of the 50 ports of ports_793.json. A role's sex is m, f or any (either; the forge makes 'any' a man until it learns to draw one). Realm ids are those of ports_793.json. A people is who a person is (name, tongue, faith); the eight cultures of wording_793.json and reputation_793.json (frankish, frisian, english, norse, slavic, baltic, finnic_rus, gaelic) still decide the words on the port menu and how a deed is weighed, by trade region. has_mint is as in 793; a mint that opens later is in the port's note with its year. (?) marks what is not verified. Tongues and faiths are game ids (tongues_793.json, night two, gives the kin table). Edit freely; the loader checks it when the game starts.
about_feeling_words: the lowest feeling (-100..100) that earns each word: shunned below -50, wary -50..-20, cool -20..0, easy 0..20, friendly 20..50, fast friend from 50 (npc_text_encounters.md 2.5)

tollman.title: the toll man
tollman.note: The king's or count's man who takes the toll (teloneum) on sales: a tenth at Dorestad and Quentovic (the zone's toll in trade_rules.json). Frank or Frisian at Dorestad, Christian, speaking the port's tongue.

moneyer.title: the moneyer
moneyer.note: Strikes the king's coin and changes old and foreign silver, at a loss to you. Offa's pennies carry their moneyers' names (Eoba, Ibba and others); Frankish coin carries the mint's name only. Frankfurt 794: the new deniers to be taken in every place; Thionville 805: coin struck only at the palace (chronicle_793.json 794-06-frankfurt-new-denier, 805-12-thionville-coin). Only where the port has a mint.

reeve.title: the reeve
reeve.note: The English king's officer in a port or on an estate (gerefa): witnesses sales, takes the toll, holds the court. A wic-reeve of Lundenwic is in the laws of Hlothhere and Eadric c. 16 (673-685); the king's reeve Beaduheard rode down to the first three ships of the Northmen at Portland and was killed (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 787 for 789; his name from Æthelweard). English realms only: in Frankish ports use tollman, lords_man or count.

harbour_master.title: the keeper of the port
harbour_master.note: Whoever says where a ship lies and answers for the landing; no single word for him in 793. At Birka a prefect, Herigar, 'a counsellor of the king' (Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 11, Robinson 1921); at Sliaswic a count of the place, Hovi (c. 31); in the Channel ports the king's procurator, Abbot Gervold, taking 'tributes and tolls in divers ports and cities, chiefly at Quentawich' (Gesta abbatum Fontanellensium c. 12, our rendering).

count.title: the count
count.note: The Frankish king's count (comes) over a district: holds the court, leads the levy, and holds the house's debt of 480 d (trade_rules.json start; the user's decision of 26 Sep 2026: the debt-holder is a Frankish count). Among the English an ealdorman, among the Danes and Northmen a jarl: use chief there.

steward.title: the steward
steward.note: Keeps a lord's hall, stores and tallies and speaks for him in small things: the steward (iudex, villicus) of a royal estate in the Capitulare de villis (c. 800); the steward of a chief's hall gives riddles in riddles_793.json.

lords_man.title: the lord's man
lords_man.note: A sworn, armed man of a count, bishop, ealdorman, jarl or king: Frankish vassus, English thegn, a Dane of the king's following. He collects, escorts, searches and carries word. All free men over twelve swore fidelity to the emperor in 802 (chronicle_793.json 802-spring-oath-of-802).

kings_man.title: the king's man
kings_man.note: An officer sent by the king himself. Frankish missi dominici ride in pairs, a churchman and a count, strangers to the district (the capitulary of 802); the English king's thegns and reeves. They search for forbidden goods: byrnies leaving the realm (Herstal 779), arms to the Slavs and Avars (Thionville 805), arms and horses to the Northmen on pain of death (Pitres 864): trade_rules.json laws.

king.title: the king
king.note: A king at his hall on a feast, seen across the fire and spoken to through his men (Design/content/BRIEF.md). Named kings only: they are in the spine's cast or a region's people with their real years; the forge should not make one.

chief.title: the chief
chief.note: A lord of a district among the peoples without counts: a Danish or Norse chieftain or jarl, a Wendish prince (dux in the Annales regni Francorum: Thrasco of the Obodrites), a lord of the Este, each of whose strongholds has its king (Wulfstan, c. 890: texts_793.json wulfstan).

lawman.title: the lawman
lawman.note: One who knows the law by heart and says it at the thing or the court: the Frisian wise men Wlemar and Saxmund whose judgements close the Lex Frisionum (c. 802). The Norse lawspeaker by that name is attested later (?).

priest.title: the priest
priest.note: A mass-priest of a church or a mission: says the hours, baptises, buries, and hears what everyone tells him. The Admonitio generalis (789) orders priests to know and preach the creed and the Lord's Prayer. In a heathen port a priest is a visitor: Birka from 829, Sliaswic from about 850 (Rimbert c. 11, 24).

bishop.title: the bishop
bishop.note: A bishop or archbishop at his see: Traiectum, Colonia, Mogontia, Rotomagus, Eoforwic, Lindisfarena, Dommoc, Canterbury by Fordwic. The real ones are named with their years in Design/content/spine.json (cast) and in the regions' places files; the forge should not make one.

abbot.title: the abbot
abbot.note: Head of a monastery (Rule of St Benedict c. 2). Many were the king's men, holding an abbey as an office: Gervold of Saint-Wandrille took the king's tolls (Gesta abbatum Fontanellensium c. 12); Alcuin held Saint Martin's at Tours from 796.

abbess.title: the abbess
abbess.note: Head of a house of nuns or of a double house of men and women: Hild's Streonaeshalch (Bede, Historia ecclesiastica IV.23); Charlemagne's sister Gisela at Chelles. Often a king's kinswoman.

monk.title: the monk
monk.note: A brother of a monastery, or one on the road with letters or books. He speaks the tongue he was born to; Latin is for the page and the liturgy (npc_text_encounters.md 2.6). Guests are received as Christ (Rule of St Benedict c. 53).

nun.title: the nun
nun.note: A sister of a nunnery or a double house. English nuns copied books and sent them oversea: Boniface asked Abbess Eadburg for the Epistles of Peter written in gold (letter of about 735) (?).

guest_master.title: the guest-master
guest_master.note: The brother who has the care of guests, who are lodged apart from the community (Rule of St Benedict c. 53): bread, ale and a bed, no meat in Lent, and letters to carry (npc_text_encounters.md sample 5).

porter.title: the porter
porter.note: The old brother at the gate, who answers every knock with 'Deo gratias' or a blessing (Rule of St Benedict c. 66). The formula is Latin; what he says next is his own tongue.

cellarer.title: the cellarer
cellarer.note: The brother who buys and keeps the house's stores (Rule of St Benedict c. 31), so the monk a merchant deals with: fish for Lent, wine, wax, salt, oil.

scribe.title: the scribe
scribe.note: Writes books and charters: Lindisfarena, Gyrwe, Eoforwic, Christ Church by Fordwic, Traiectum, Saint-Denis by Parisius. His jokes are the margin's: cold hands, bad ink, a long day (Design/content/BRIEF.md rule 3).

schoolmaster.title: the schoolmaster
schoolmaster.note: Master of a cathedral or minster school: Alcuin's at Eoforwic until 782, Gregory's at Traiectum where Liudger learned (Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.9-12). Gives the Latin riddles of Aldhelm and Symphosius (riddles_793.json).

clerk.title: the clerk
clerk.note: A cleric in a lord's or bishop's service who writes and reckons: the churchman of a pair of missi, a clerk of the mint or of the palace (riddles_793.json), the clerk with a king's ship (npc_text_encounters.md sample 18).

merchant.title: the merchant
merchant.note: A trader with goods and a ship or a share in one (negotiator, mercator; Old English mangere). Ælfric's merchant, c. 995: 'I go aboard my ship with my cargo... and buy precious things that are not produced in this land' (texts_793.json aelfric_merchant, the game's own rendering). In 793 the Frisians are the carriers: 'a certain Frisian merchant' at York (Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.11).

factor.title: the factor
factor.note: A house's own man left in a far port to buy, store and send word: a game office (the winter choice 'a factor in a far port', research_indie_and_concept.md 4.4). The nearest things in the sources: the Frisians living at Eoforwic until about 773 (Altfrid I.11), the Frisian quarter of Mogontia (Annales Fuldenses 886), an abbey's own traders.

skipper.title: the skipper
skipper.note: The master of a ship met in port: he steers her and answers for her crew and lading (Old English steorman; Old Norse styrimathr on 11th-century rune stones).

master.title: the master
master.note: The master of a ship hailed at sea, fixed to that ship (npc_text_encounters.md 4.2, card sea.hail.master, and sample 13).

pilot.title: the pilot
pilot.note: A local man who knows one bar, one channel and its tides, hired for a tide or a day (Old English ladmann, a guide (?)). There are no charts: the way is in his head, and he says it by marks, soundings and the colour of the water (research_trade_seasons_and_hints.md 4).

steersman.title: the steersman
steersman.note: The man at the side rudder: the first of the crew's seats at the council before a crossing (npc_text_encounters.md sample 19).

mate.title: the mate
mate.note: The man who speaks for the crew to the merchant about shares and pay (npc_text_encounters.md sample 20). A game seat: a crew of four has no such rank in the sources.

lookout.title: the lookout
lookout.note: The sharpest eyes aboard, in the bow: a crew seat (npc_text_encounters.md sample 19).

crewman.title: the hand
crewman.note: One of the four men of a Gislinge boat (7.7 m, four men: Design/content/BRIEF.md), each with a trait, a want, a fear, a home port and a faith (research_indie_and_concept.md 4.5).

sailor.title: the sailor
sailor.note: A hand of another ship, ashore: 'Worse food for the journey he brings not afield than an over-drinking of ale' (Hávamál 11, Bellows 1923: texts_793.json havamal_011); the drunk sailors of sample 10.

survivor.title: the survivor
survivor.note: Someone taken off a wreck or a sandbank (npc_text_encounters.md sample 14). Ælfric's merchant: 'sometimes I suffer shipwreck with the loss of all my things, barely escaping alive' (texts_793.json aelfric_merchant).

shipwright.title: the shipwright
shipwright.note: Builds and mends clinker boats with axe, rivets, tar and moss: the Gislinge boat herself. Alfred's long ships of 896 were shaped neither like the Frisian nor like the Danish ones, so both patterns were known (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 897 for 896). Riddles: a Gotland shipwright at Paviken (riddles_793.json).

smith.title: the smith
smith.note: Iron worker: tools, rivets, knives, and in the Rhineland the sword blades the law forbids to leave the realm. A king's smith has his own price in Æthelberht's laws c. 7 (about 600); a Gotland smith's whole tool chest survives (Mästermyr, about 1000).

goldsmith.title: the goldsmith
goldsmith.note: Works silver and gold, tests coin, cuts hacksilver and weighs it on folding scales with lead weights; the man to ask what a strange coin is worth (riddles_793.json: Gestumblindi 4, the goldsmith's hammer, bought at Sliesthorp or Ripa).

craftsman.title: the craftsman
craftsman.note: A worker in antler, horn, bone, amber, glass beads, leather, wood or clay in the craft plots of a trading place: Ripa's bead and comb makers, Dorestad's amber workers (Research/dorestad_c800_notes.md), Gipeswic's potters, a tanner at Lundenwic, a horn-worker and a bowyer (riddles_793.json).

rune_carver.title: the rune-carver
rune_carver.note: Cuts runes in wood, bone and stone: English runes on the Northumbrian crosses and Cuthbert's coffin (698), the short Norse row of 16 runes from about 800 (runes_793.json). A Northumbrian rune-carver and a Gotland stone-carver give riddles (riddles_793.json).

weaver.title: the weaver
weaver.note: Cloth is women's work on the upright loom: Frisian cloth (pallia fresonica), the English cloaks whose length Charlemagne complained of to Offa in 796, the women's workrooms of a royal estate with their wool, flax, woad and madder (Capitulare de villis c. 43, 49).

salter.title: the salter
salter.note: Rakes the pans or boils the brine: the monks' pans at Herio (Noirmoutier) and the bay salt of the Loire, the brine of Droitwich in Mercia (goods_793.json sea_salt, brine_salt). Salt is dearest at the Martinmas slaughter (research_trade_seasons_and_hints.md 1).

fisherman.title: the fisherman
fisherman.note: Ælfric's fisherman (c. 995) takes eels, pike, herring and salmon and will not go after whales, because it is a risky thing (Ælfric's Colloquy, our rendering). He knows his own channel and where it moved last winter (npc_text_encounters.md sample 17).

hunter.title: the hunter
hunter.note: Ælfric's king's hunter with nets, hounds and a boar spear (c. 995); in the north the trapper who brings marten, beaver and squirrel, and the Finnas who pay Ohthere in skins, feathers and ship's rope (texts_793.json ohthere).

fowler.title: the fowler
fowler.note: Takes wildfowl with nets, snares, lime and a hawk (Ælfric's fowler, c. 995); eggs and down on the skerries (riddles_793.json: fowlers at Gipeswic, Uppsalir and Ogvaldsnes).

farmer.title: the farmer
farmer.note: A free man with land or a lord's tenant, at market with grain, a beast, honey or wax: Ælfric's ploughman, it is hard work, because I am not free (Ælfric's Colloquy, c. 995, our rendering); a ploughman of Thanet and a beekeeper give riddles (riddles_793.json).

farm_wife.title: the farm wife
farm_wife.note: Keeps the dairy, the hens, the garden and the loom, and sells butter, cheese and eggs (riddles_793.json: a farm wife at Fordwic, one with an angelica bed at Ogvaldsnes; a market woman selling onions at Lundenwic).

herdsman.title: the herdsman
herdsman.note: Shepherd, swineherd, oxherd or drover: Ælfric's shepherd stands over his flock with dogs lest wolves devour them (Ælfric's Colloquy, c. 995, our rendering); the cattle drovers and dealers of Ripa, the swineherd of the king's estate at Hleidr (riddles_793.json).

carter.title: the carter
carter.note: Takes goods inland from the landing by ox-cart or pack-horse (riddles_793.json: a carter at Ripa); the men who haul ships and goods across the neck from the Schlei to the Treene at Sliesthorp.

ferryman.title: the ferryman
ferryman.note: Keeps a crossing with a logboat or a flat barge and sees everyone who passes (riddles_793.json: a ferryman on the Schlei). A toll may be asked only where a bridge or a ferry gives help (capitularies of 809: chronicle_793.json 809-sunday-markets).

alewife.title: the ale-wife
alewife.note: The woman who brews and sells ale by the landing: brewing is household work and women's. Say ale-house, never tavern or inn. Priests are told to keep out of drinking-houses (tabernae) in the Carolingian capitularies (?); an ale-house (ealahus) is in English law by III Æthelred 1 (about 997). Ale and mead are everyone's; wine is the lord's and the Mass's.

host.title: the host
host.note: A householder who lodges strangers and answers for them: in Kent a man who keeps a guest three nights answers for him (Hlothhere and Eadric c. 15) (?). 'Fire he needs who with frozen knees has come from the cold without' (Hávamál 3, Bellows 1923: texts_793.json havamal_003).

widow.title: the widow
widow.note: A woman who holds her dead husband's house, storehouse or share in a ship. Frideburg of Birka, rich and old, had her daughter Catla sell all and carry the silver to Dorstadt for the poor, where 'there are... many churches, priests, and clergy, and a multitude of poor people' (Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 20, Robinson 1921).

singer.title: the singer
singer.note: One who tells the deeds of old kings to a hall for his meat: Old English scop and gleoman. Bernlef, a blind man of Helewyret in Frisia, was loved by his neighbours because he 'knew well how to tell the deeds of the men of old and the wars of kings' (Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.25: antiquorum actus regumque certamina; our rendering). The role is the man and what he knows; the game's music is set aside for now (the user, 4 Oct 2026).

skald.title: the skald
skald.note: A Norse king's or chief's poet, keeper of the hall's lays and riddles (riddles_793.json: the skalds of Hleidr, Uppsalir, Ogvaldsnes and Birka). The lays were written down in the 13th century and are older in substance; the first skald with a name is Bragi the Old, 9th century.

setter.title: the riddle-setter
setter.note: Whoever sets a riddle to a guest (npc_text_encounters.md sample 24 and 2.9); the riddles, their answers and where each is had are riddles_793.json. The setter who leads from port to port is the spine's thread 'riddle_road'.

interpreter.title: the interpreter
interpreter.note: One who speaks two tongues (Old English wealhstod). King Oswald himself put Bishop Aidan's Irish into English for his thegns (Bede, Historia ecclesiastica III.3); the legates' decrees of 786 were read out in Latin and in the people's tongue (theodisce).

pilgrim.title: the pilgrim
pilgrim.note: Bound for Rome, 'the residence of the holy apostles', or a saint's tomb, by Quentovic and the hospice of Saint-Josse. Charlemagne to Offa, 796: let pilgrims 'go peaceably without any molestation', but those 'not seeking the cause of religion, but that of gain' are to 'pay the customary tolls in proper places' (William of Malmesbury, tr. Giles 1847).

slave_dealer.title: the dealer in captives
slave_dealer.note: Buys captives where war or raiders sell them and carries them to where the law does not ask. A Frisian bought the captive thegn Imma in London in 679 (Bede, Historia ecclesiastica IV.22); Anskar bought Danish and Slav boys to train them for God's service (Rimbert c. 15). Christians may not be sold out of the realm (trade_rules.json laws; reputation_793.json sold_captives).

captive.title: the captive
captive.note: A person held for sale or ransom: the youths of Lindisfarne carried off by the heathen, whom Alcuin hoped King Charles could help to recover (Alcuin to Higbald, 793: MGH Epistolae IV no. 20), a Saxon taken in the wars, a Wend, anyone taken at sea (goods_793.json captives).

hostage.title: the hostage
hostage.note: Given by a people or a lord as surety and kept far from home by a bishop, abbot or count: the Saxons gave hostages in 794 and 1,600 in 798 (chronicle_793.json 794-autumn-sintfeld, 798-summer-minden); a list of Saxon hostages to be brought to Mainz survives from about 805 (Indiculus obsidum Saxonum Moguntiam deducendorum).

beggar.title: the beggar
beggar.note: One of the poor at a church door or on the strand: Dorstadt's 'multitude of poor people' (Rimbert c. 20). In the famine of 793-794 the roads are full of them (chronicle_793.json 793-great-famine). Alms are a deed (reputation_793.json gave_alms).

child.title: the child
child.note: A child of the port who runs errands, minds a boat and tells what he saw. A child given to a monastery with his parents' gift is an oblate (Rule of St Benedict c. 59): the boys of Lindisfarne were such.

wise_woman.title: the wise woman
wise_woman.note: A woman who knows herbs, births, charms and signs, and whom the priest preaches against. The Indiculus superstitionum et paganiarum (a list of about 743, copied about 800) names amulets and knots (10), incantations (12), auguries from birds, horses and dung (13) and women who believe they command the moon (30). In the north a seeress with a staff: the saga accounts are 13th-century, but an iron staff lay with the women of the Oseberg ship burial of 834 (?).

leech.title: the leech
leech.note: One who lets blood, sets bones and gives herbs (Old English laece). Bald's Leechbook is a 9th-century English book of such cures; a monastery's infirmarer is the nearest in most ports (npc_text_encounters.md sample 21).

raider_chief.title: the chief of the raiders
raider_chief.note: The leader of a ship's crew or a small fleet that takes by force: 'heathen men' and 'Northmen' in the annals, never 'Vikings' as a people (Design/content/BRIEF.md rule 2). He parleys, sells loot and captives and takes tribute: the Frisians paid 100 pounds of silver in 810 (chronicle_793.json 810-summer-frisia-raid-810).

raider.title: the raider
raider.note: One of a raider chief's crew: a farmer's son home by the autumn. Raiders go out about the first of May and are home before October (Plans/ai_fleets.md, in economy_and_trade.md 1.3).

warrior.title: the warrior
warrior.note: An armed man of a hall or a fort who is no officer: Bebbanburg's rock, a Danish king's following at Sliesthorp, the fort above Birka (riddles_793.json: a man of Birka's garrison with a gaming bag).

envoy.title: the envoy
envoy.note: One who carries a ruler's word and waits for the answer: Godfred of the Danes 'sent word by merchants' in 809 (chronicle_793.json 809-badenfliot); a raider's envoy who names a town's share (npc_text_encounters.md sample 9).

commander.title: the captain of the king's ship
commander.note: Commands a ship set to keep a coast: Charlemagne had ships built and watches set at the river mouths against the Northmen from 800 and again in 810-811 (Einhard, Vita Karoli c. 17; chronicle_793.json 811-10-boulogne-capitulary); Alfred's long ships, 896 (npc_text_encounters.md sample 18).

owner.title: the owner
owner.note: The owner of silver put in the ground when raiders came, or the heir who was told the place (npc_text_encounters.md 1.5, 2.10 and sample 25; hoards_793.json).

about_peoples: who each people is, for the writers: frankish = Franks of the Rhine, Meuse and Scheldt, speaking Frankish; romance = the Romance-speaking people of Neustria, the Loire and Aquitaine (Franks by realm, 'Romans' by speech: the two tongues are sworn side by side at Strasbourg in 842); frisian = Frisians from the Scheldt to the Weser; saxon = the Old Saxons between Rhine and Elbe, baptised by force since 785; english = Mercians, West Saxons, Kentishmen, East Angles, Northumbrians; danish = Danes of Jutland, the islands and Skane; norse = Northmen of Vestfold and the west coast; svea = the Svear of Lake Malaren; gute = the people of Gotland (to the Svear's lordship by Wulfstan's day, c. 890); wendish = the Slavs of the Baltic coast, Obodrites and Wilzi; slavic = the Slavs of Lake Ilmen and the Volkhov; baltic = Prussians (the Este) and Curonians; finnic_rus = the Finnic peoples round Ladoga; irish = the Irish of Ireland; gaelic = the Gaels of Dal Riata and the Isles. For standing and the port's words each counts as its culture: romance and saxon as frankish, danish, svea and gute as norse, wendish as slavic, irish as gaelic.

dorestad.note: A Frisian emporium in the Frankish realm: the mint in the upper town (Madelinus, then Carolingian coin) and the king's toll (npc_text_encounters.md 1.1). 'Many churches, priests, and clergy, and a multitude of poor people' by the 850s (Rimbert c. 20). Gone after 863.

traiectum.note: Willibrord's see: Saint Martin's and the school where Liudger learned under Gregory (Altfrid I.9-10). The bishop in 793 is Hamacar (790-806 in the bishops' list) (?). English-born clergy since Willibrord and Boniface. No mint in 793; the bishops strike coin from the 10th century (?).

walichrum.note: The beach market on Walcheren. Willibrord broke an idol here and its keeper struck him with a sword (Alcuin, Vita Willibrordi c. 14); the Northmen take the island in 837 and Lothar grants it to Harald in 841 (chronicle_793.json).

witla.note: A Frisian market at the Maas mouth, burned by the Northmen in 836 (Annales Fuldenses 836: emporium Witla) and not rebuilt.

medemelacha.note: West Frisian market on the Almere shore, on the inland way north from Dorestad; Frankish, and so Christian by law, since about 719, when Radbod died (?).

wijnaldum.note: A great terp of Westergo, an old seat of Frisian lords (?); in the bishop of Utrecht's care. The old customs are a living memory: Frisia west of the Lauwers was conquered in 734.

doccinga.note: Where Boniface and his companions were killed on 5 June 754; a church stands on the place. Willehad preached here about 766-770 and Liudger for seven years until Widukind's rising of 784 drove the priests out (Altfrid I.17-21).

emuthon.note: Emisga, one of the five districts given to Liudger in 787 (Altfrid I.22). CAUTION for 793: the East Frisians rose under Unno and Eilrat about 792-793, burned the churches and drove the priests out; Liudger was back 'after the circle of a year' (Altfrid I.22). Gate a card on the rising with year = 793.

daventre.note: Lebuin's church on the IJssel at the Saxon border, burned by Saxons and rebuilt by Liudger over the saint's grave about 775-776 (Altfrid I.13-15). Franks and Saxons both live here. A mint only from about 1000 (?).

noviomagus.note: The king's palace above the Waal: Charles keeps Easter here in some years, and the exiled King Eardwulf of Northumbria comes to him here in 808 (Annales regni Francorum 808). Clerks of the palace (riddles_793.json).

quentovic.note: The Channel emporium on the Canche: the king's toll, 'chiefly at Quentawich', under Abbot Gervold from 787 (Gesta abbatum Fontanellensium c. 12), a mint, and the crossing of English pilgrims; Alcuin has the cell of Saint-Josse nearby as a hospice from about 792 (?). Its merchants are Franks, English ('Saxons') and Frisians. Sacked in 842.

rotomagus.note: The archbishop's city at the tide's reach on the Seine, with a mint; Saint-Wandrille (Fontenelle), Gervold's abbey, lies downstream. Sacked in 841; from 911 the seat of Rollo and his Northmen (chronicle_793.json 841-05-rouen-sacked, 911-rollo-rouen).

parisius.note: The Seine city and the abbey of Saint-Denis, whose fair from 9 October draws Saxon (English) and Frisian merchants: the tolls of the fair were confirmed to the abbey by Pippin in 753 (fairs_793.json). Sacked on Easter Day 845.

ganda.note: Saint Bavo's and Saint Peter's abbeys where the Lys meets the Scheldt; Einhard is lay abbot of both from about 815. Charlemagne inspects the fleet built here in 811 (Annales regni Francorum 811). The great army winters here in 879-880.

andoverpis.note: A fort and landing on the Scheldt with a church of the Utrecht mission (Willibrord held a church here from 726) (?); burned by the Northmen in 836 (Annales Fuldenses 836).

colonia.note: The old Roman city: Archbishop Hildebold (787-818) is the king's arch-chaplain; Liudger was ordained priest here on 7 July 777. Wine, glass, pottery and the smiths of the Rhineland; a mint. Burned by the Northmen in the winter of 881-882.

mogontia.note: Boniface's see at the Main's mouth, a mint, and a Frisian merchants' quarter: 'the best part of the city, where the Frisians lived' burned in 886 (Annales Fuldenses). Saxon hostages are ordered brought here about 805. Ibrahim ibn Yaqub sees Samarkand dirhams and eastern spices here in 965.

diusburg.note: A Frankish market at the Ruhr's mouth, where the road east into Saxony (the Hellweg) leaves the Rhine; Liudger's abbey of Werden (from about 799) is a few hours up the Ruhr. The Northmen winter here in 883-884 (Regino). A mint only from the 10th century (?).

lundenwic.note: Bede's mart of many peoples who come to it by land and sea (Historia ecclesiastica II.3), a Mercian town in 793 with a mint and the king's wic-reeve. A Frisian bought a captive here in 679 (Bede IV.22). Stormed in 851; Alfred holds it from 886.

hamwic.note: The West Saxons' wic on the Itchen, trading with the Seine and Quentovic. Earlier sceattas are laid to it; no mint is sure in 793 (?). King Beorhtric of Wessex (786-802) is Offa's son-in-law. Plundered in 842 (Nithard IV.3) (?) and sacked in 980 (chronicle_793.json 980-raids-southampton-chester).

gipeswic.note: The East Angles' wic on the Orwell and its potters. The East Anglian pennies of Offa and of King Æthelberht, beheaded by Offa in 794, were probably struck here (?). Ravaged in 991 before Maldon.

eoforwic.note: The Northumbrian kings' and archbishops' city: the minster, its school and library (Alcuin's until 782), the kings' coin. Frisian merchants lived here until about 773, when one of them killed a nobleman's son and all fled (Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.11-12). Taken by the great army on 1 November 866.

sarre.note: The Kentish toll place on the Wantsum: Kentish and Mercian kings freed ships of the Thanet minsters from the toll at Sarre and Fordwic in 8th-century charters (riddles_793.json rw_toll_fordwic).

fordwic.note: Canterbury's landing on the Stour. The mint, the archbishop (Æthelheard, 792-805) and the scribes of Christ Church are in the city, an hour's walk up the river road: Offa's and the archbishop's pennies are struck there.

dofras.note: The short crossing under the Roman lighthouse (Aldhelm's riddle of the lighthouse: riddles_793.json riddle_aldhelm_92_farus) and the minster of Saint Martin.

lindisfarena.note: Cuthbert's island, a bishop's see: Higbald, 780/1-803. Heathen men fell on it on 8 June 793, killed some brethren and carried off others, youths among them (Alcuin's letters; Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 793). The community stays until 875.

bebbanburg.note: The Northumbrian kings' rock, in sight of Lindisfarne; Saint Oswald's arm lay in its church (Bede, Historia ecclesiastica III.6). King Æthelred (790-796) is murdered on 18 April 796; Eardwulf reigns from May 796.

gyrwe.note: Bede's monastery on the Tyne, one house with Wearmouth, and its books. Heathen men plundered the monastery at Donemuthe in 794; their leader was killed and a storm broke their ships (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 794), which is usually taken to be this house (?).

streonaeshalch.note: Hild's double house of monks and nuns on the cliff above the Esk, where the Easter question was settled in 664 (Bede, Historia ecclesiastica III.25, IV.23); jet from the cliffs (goods_793.json jet). Wasted about 867 (?).

dommoc.note: The East Angles' southern bishop's see since Felix (Bede, Historia ecclesiastica II.15); whether Dommoc is Dunwich is not sure (?). East Anglia is under Offa from 794.

legacaestir.note: The old city of the legions on the Dee, Mercian, facing the Welsh and the Irish Sea; lead from the hills behind (riddles_793.json: a lead-miner's reeve). A waste 'chester' the Danes hold in 893 (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 894); restored in 907 and a busy mint in the 10th century (?).

hi.note: Columba's island, head of his family of monasteries. Abbot Bresal dies in 801; plundered in 795, burned in 802, sixty-eight of the community killed in 806; Abbot Cellach builds Kells from 807 (Annals of Ulster: chronicle_793.json).

duiblinn.note: A church by the black pool on the Liffey. From 841 a ship-fort of the Northmen and then a Norse town and slave market: after 841 its people are norse with irish among them, and its first coin is struck in 997 (chronicle_793.json 841-duiblinn-longphort, 997-dublin-coins). The table has no years yet: gate such cards with port.id = duiblinn and the year.

ripa.note: The Danes' oldest market, laid out in plots about 700-710, busy in summer with Frisian ships: beads, combs, amber, cattle. Whether the Wodan-and-monster sceattas were struck here is argued (?); the game has no coin of the north before about 825. Anskar gets leave for a church here in the late 850s (Rimbert c. 32).

sliesthorp.note: A market at the head of the Schlei. Godfred comes here with his fleet in 804 and brings Reric's merchants here in 808 (Annales regni Francorum): from 808 Wends, Saxons and Frisians live beside the Danes. Its own coin from about 825 and a church from about 850 (Rimbert c. 24). The table has no years yet, so has_mint stays false: gate a card about the mint with port.id = sliesthorp and year >= 825.

reric.note: The Obodrites' emporium on the Wismar bay, which by the tolls it paid was of great profit to Godfred's kingdom (Annales regni Francorum 808, our rendering): Danes and Saxons trade here among the Wends. Destroyed in 808; Prince Thrasco is murdered here in 809.

skiringssal.note: Vestfold's market (Kaupang), from about 800, busy in summer; Ohthere's 'port which men call Sciringes heal' about 890 (texts_793.json ohthere). Vestfold is under the Danish kings in 813 (Annales regni Francorum).

birka.note: The Svear's market on Bjorko, under a prefect of the king (Herigar, baptised about 830) and a thing where the king must ask the people (Rimbert c. 11, 19, 26-27). Silver by weight; dirhams from about 800. Men of Birka have been to Dorstadt (c. 27). Abandoned about 975.

helgo.note: An older craft and trading place in Malaren, giving way to Birka by about 800: bronze-casters' moulds, and far-fetched things in its soil (an Irish crozier head, a small Buddha from India).

uppsalir.note: The Svear kings' seat and the great mounds. The temple, the three gods and the nine-yearly feast are Adam of Bremen's account of about 1075 (Gesta IV.26-27): LATER, do not put his words in a mouth of 793. The Disting, a thing and market in late winter, is in Snorri (13th century) (?).

paviken.note: A Gotland harbour of shipwrights and smiths. Wulfstan, about 890: Gotland belongs to the Svear (texts_793.json wulfstan). More silver has been found on Gotland than anywhere in the north: the Spillings hoard, 67 kg, was buried after 870 (riddles_793.json rw_hoard_spillings).

ahus.note: A market at the Helge river's mouth in Skane, with bead and comb makers. Wulfstan, about 890: Skane belongs to Denmark (texts_793.json wulfstan).

truso.note: The amber market of the Este on Lake Druzno, seven days and nights' sail from Hedeby (Wulfstan, about 890: texts_793.json wulfstan): each stronghold has its king, the rich drink mare's milk and the poor and the slaves mead, and the dead lie unburned for a month while their goods are raced for. Danish craftsmen and traders live here (the digs at Janow Pomorski) (?).

grobin.note: A settlement of Gotlanders and Svear among the Curonians, about 650-850 (its grave fields). The Cori 'had in former time been in subjection to the Swedes'; the Svear take Seeburg and besiege Apulia about 854 (Rimbert c. 30, Robinson 1921). Seeburg may be this place (?).

aldeigjuborg.note: The gate to the east on the Volkhov, from about 753 (its oldest timbers): Svear and Gotlanders, Slavs of Lake Ilmen, and the Finnic peoples of the woods who bring the furs (a finnic_rus person may be named on a card; the table gives them men's names only). A hoard of dirhams here closes with a coin of 786 (riddles_793.json rw_hoard_ladoga).

ogvaldsnes.note: A chief's seat on the Karmsund, the sheltered way north, where every ship must pass. The three ships that came to Portland about 789 were of 'Hæretha land', Hordaland, just north of here (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 787). Insular church metalwork lies in 9th-century graves along this coast.

hleidr.note: The Danish kings' hall on Zealand, the Heorot of Beowulf by most reckonings (?); great halls of the 7th to 10th centuries have been dug here. Thietmar of Merseburg (about 1015) tells of a sacrifice here every nine years in January, ended in 934: LATER, mark it so.

namnetis.note: The Loire city at the Breton march: salt and wine. Its count keeps the march against the Bretons. Stormed on Saint John's day 843 and Bishop Gunhard killed in his church (chronicle_793.json 843-06-24-nantes-sacked). A mint for the later Carolingians (?).

herio.note: Saint Philibert's island monastery and its salt pans. Northmen come to the islands of Aquitaine in 799 (Alcuin's letter of that year); the monks leave the island each summer from 819 and for good in 836, carrying the saint inland (Ermentarius).

burdigala.note: The Garonne city of Aquitaine, under King Louis (Charles's son, king of Aquitaine from 781): wine. Gascons to the south. A mint (?). Taken by the Northmen in 848.
